Designing a Distributed Message Queue (Kafka)

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Advanced Topics: Partitioned Log, Consumer Groups, Exactly-Once Delivery, Replication, Ordering Asked at: Google, Amazon, Microsoft, LinkedIn, Uber, Confluent Prerequisites:Scalability, Database Replication, and Leader Election

1. Understanding the Problem

A distributed message queue decouples producers from consumers — services publish events without knowing who consumes them, and consumers process at their own pace without blocking producers. The hard engineering problems: guaranteeing no message loss even when brokers crash, maintaining strict ordering within a partition while allowing parallel consumption, and achieving exactly-once semantics in a distributed system where networks are unreliable.💡 Exactly-once semantics = every message gets processed one time, never zero and never twice. It is the hardest guarantee to give because a lost network reply makes “did my write land?” genuinely unanswerable. Learn more →

Real examples: Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Google Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ, Apache Pulsar, Redpanda.

2. Naive First Cut

In-memory FIFO queue on a single server. Producer pushes, consumer pops.

Why this breaks:

  • Server crash = all messages lost (in-memory, no persistence)
  • Single server limits throughput to one machine’s I/O (~100K msg/sec)
  • One consumer means no parallel processing — throughput bottlenecked by consumer speed
  • No replay — once a message is consumed, it’s gone (can’t reprocess after a bug fix)
  • No ordering guarantees when you add multiple consumers
  • No backpressure — if consumers are slow, memory fills up and the server runs out of memory (OOM) and dies💡 Backpressure = letting a slow consumer push back so producers slow down, instead of the buffer quietly growing until the machine dies. Without it the only limit on the queue is the size of RAM.

The rest of the doc evolves this into a replicated, partitioned, persistent log with consumer groups.

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • LinkedIn Kafka - Invented the partitioned commit log model. Messages are appended to an immutable, ordered log. Consumers track their own position (offset) and can replay from any point. This single abstraction replaced dozens of point-to-point queues at LinkedIn. (LinkedIn Engineering)
  • Amazon Kinesis Shards - Similar to Kafka partitions but with a different scaling model: throughput is provisioned per shard (1MB/sec write, 2MB/sec read). Auto-scaling splits hot shards when write capacity is exceeded.
  • Google Pub/Sub - Separates the concept of “topic” from “subscription.” Multiple subscriptions to the same topic each get independent message delivery — no consumer group coordination needed. Messages are stored until acknowledged (pull-based with ACK deadlines).
  • Redpanda (Raft-based replication) - Replaces Kafka’s ZooKeeper-based controller with embedded Raft consensus per partition. Simplifies operations and provides stronger consistency guarantees during leader elections. (Redpanda Blog)💡 Raft = a protocol a group of machines uses to agree on one ordered list of decisions and on who is currently in charge. It is how a cluster answers “who owns partition 3 right now?” without two machines both believing it is them. Learn more →

4. Functional Requirements

Core (Top 3)

  1. Publish messages to a topic - producers write messages to named topics with guaranteed durability (acknowledged only after replication)
  2. Consume messages with ordering - consumers in a group process messages in partition order, exactly once, with the ability to replay from any offset
  3. Scale throughput horizontally - adding partitions and brokers increases capacity linearly without downtime

Below the Line

  • Message filtering (server-side tag-based routing)
  • Dead-letter queues for poison messages💡 A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is a side queue for messages that keep failing. Without one, a single unprocessable “poison” message blocks its partition forever because the consumer retries it and never gets past it.
  • Message time-to-live (TTL) and compaction (retain latest per key)
  • Transactions across multiple topics
  • Multi-region replication

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core

  • Throughput: 1M+ messages/sec per cluster (with appropriate partitions)
  • Latency: Produce-to-consume P99 (the delay that 99% of messages beat) < 10ms (within a single datacenter)💡 Averages hide the bad cases, so capacity targets are written against a high percentile. A 2ms average with a 400ms P99 means one message in a hundred is unusably slow. Learn more →
  • Durability: Zero message loss — acknowledged writes survive broker crashes
  • Ordering: Strict ordering within a partition (total order)

Below the Line

  • 7-day default retention (configurable to infinite)
  • Exactly-once semantics (with idempotent producers + transactional consumers)
  • Graceful broker addition/removal without message loss

6. Core Entities

  • Topic - a named stream that producers write to and consumers subscribe to
  • Partition - an ordered, immutable log within a topic (the unit of parallelism)
  • Message - a key-value pair with headers and a timestamp, appended at an offset
  • Offset - the position of a message within a partition (monotonically increasing integer)💡 Monotonically increasing = the number only ever goes up, never back. That is what lets a consumer store its entire progress through a partition as one integer instead of a per-message checklist.
  • ConsumerGroup - a set of consumers that collectively process a topic (each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in the group)
  • Broker - a server that stores partitions and serves produce/consume requests

7. API / System Interface

POST /v1/topics/{topic}/produce
Body: {
  "messages": [
    {"key": "user_123", "value": "{\"event\":\"purchase\",\"amount\":500}", "headers": {"trace_id": "t1"}},
    ...
  ],
  "acks": "all"  // wait for all ISR replicas
}
Response: {"offsets": [{"partition": 2, "offset": 10542}]}

POST /v1/topics/{topic}/consume
Body: {
  "group_id": "payment-processor",
  "max_messages": 100,
  "timeout_ms": 5000
}
Response: {
  "messages": [{"partition": 2, "offset": 10542, "key": "user_123", "value": "...", "timestamp": 1720000000}],
  "has_more": true
}

POST /v1/topics/{topic}/commit
Body: {"group_id": "payment-processor", "offsets": {"2": 10543}}
Response: 200 OK

Security notes: produce/consume authenticated via the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL). Access control lists (ACLs) per topic (which services can produce/consume). Encryption in-transit (Transport Layer Security, TLS) and optionally at-rest (broker disk encryption).💡 An access control list is just a per-topic table of “which service is allowed to read, which is allowed to write.” It matters here because one broker holds many teams’ topics on the same disk. Learn more →

8. High-Level Design

FR1: Publish messages (durable, replicated writes)

A producer sends a message, a broker appends it to a log on disk, and the broker acknowledges with the offset it landed at. That is the whole of publishing.

New components we need:

  1. Broker - owns a partition, appends messages to its log, hands back offsets.
  2. Partition log - an append-only file on disk. Appending is the only write operation this system ever performs, which is what makes it fast.

Flow:

  1. Producer picks a partition round-robin and sends the message to the broker that owns it
  2. Broker appends it to the end of that partition’s log file and records the offset
  3. Broker returns the offset. The producer treats that as success and moves on

Why an append-only log rather than a queue data structure? Because a sequential disk write is roughly as fast as a memory write on modern hardware, and a log never needs to delete from the middle, reorder, or rebalance. It also means a message’s position is its identity — the offset — so a consumer’s progress is a single integer rather than per-message state. Almost everything else on this page follows from that one choice.

What we have deliberately left broken. Messages are durably on disk and addressable by offset. Four things are missing, and each is a separate deep dive:

  • One copy, on one broker’s disk. If that machine’s disk dies, every unread message in the partition is gone. That is Deep Dive 2.
  • The producer does not retry. Step 3 returns an offset, and if that response is lost in flight the producer has no idea whether the append happened. As written it moves on, so the message is silently dropped — at-most-once. That is Deep Dive 1.
  • Round-robin destroys ordering per entity. Step 1 spreads a given entity’s messages across every partition, so payment_completed can be consumed before payment_created. That is Deep Dive 4.
  • Nothing bounds what a producer can send. The broker accepts whatever arrives at whatever rate. That is Deep Dive 5.

FR2: Consume messages with ordering (consumer groups)

Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in a group. This guarantees ordering within a partition while allowing parallel consumption across partitions.

New components:

  • Group Coordinator: A broker given the extra job of bookkeeping for one consumer group. It records which consumer currently owns which partition, and it is the thing that notices when a consumer stops answering. It exists because the assignment has to be agreed in one place — if each consumer picked its own partitions, two of them would pick the same one.
  • Consumer 1 / 2 / 3: Separate processes (usually separate machines) running the same application code. Each is handed its own partitions, which is how the group processes a topic in parallel without two consumers touching the same ordered log.

Flow:

  1. Consumers join a group and send heartbeats to the Group Coordinator💡 A heartbeat is a small “I’m still alive” message on a timer. It is the only way the coordinator can tell a crashed consumer apart from a slow one, and the timeout it waits is how long a dead consumer’s partitions sit unread.
  2. Coordinator assigns partitions to consumers (range or round-robin strategy)
  3. Each consumer fetches a batch from its assigned partitions in offset order
  4. The consumer commits the offset as soon as it has the batch, then processes it
  5. If a consumer crashes, the coordinator detects the missing heartbeat and reassigns its partitions to survivors
  6. Survivors resume from the last committed offset

Why one partition per consumer, rather than letting several consumers share one? Because ordering within a partition is the only ordering guarantee the log can offer, and two consumers reading the same partition concurrently would process its messages in whatever order they happened to finish. Exclusive assignment is what makes “ordered within a partition” true end to end rather than just on disk.

What we have deliberately left broken. Consumption scales across partitions and survives a consumer dying. Step 4 is the problem, and the direction of the bug matters:

Committing the offset before processing means a consumer that crashes mid-batch has already declared those messages done. The survivor resumes after them, and that batch is never processed by anyone — silently, with no error and no dead letter. We have built a queue that loses messages on consumer failure, which is the one thing a queue exists not to do.

Committing after processing instead would trade this for duplicates, which is a better trade and still not a solution. That whole question is Deep Dive 1.

FR3: Scale throughput (partitioning)

Throughput scales linearly with partitions. More partitions = more parallel producers and consumers.

Flow:

  1. Topic created with N partitions distributed across brokers
  2. Each partition handles ~100K msg/sec (limited by disk I/O of one broker)
  3. Adding more partitions = more total throughput (4 partitions = ~400K msg/sec)
  4. Consumer group scales to N consumers (one per partition) for maximum parallelism
  5. Adding more consumers beyond N provides no benefit (idle consumers)
  6. To scale further: add partitions + brokers (online, no downtime)

Why is the partition the unit of parallelism and not the message? Because ordering is per partition. If messages were handed out individually, nothing could promise an order to anyone. The partition count is therefore a ceiling on consumer parallelism that you choose up front, which is why over-partitioning slightly is normal practice — adding partitions later changes which partition a key hashes to.

What we have deliberately left broken. Throughput now scales by adding partitions and brokers. Two things this does not address:

  • The log grows without bound. Nothing deletes anything. At 1M msg/sec and ~1KB a message that is 1GB/sec, about 86TB a day, appended forever to disks that are not infinite. The system works perfectly until the disks fill, and then every partition on that broker stops accepting writes at once. That is Deep Dive 3.
  • Partitions balance messages, not load. Once Deep Dive 4 routes by key to recover ordering, an entity that is far busier than the others concentrates on one partition — and that partition is capped at the ~100K msg/sec of a single broker no matter how many partitions the topic has. Adding partitions cannot fix it, which is the same shape of problem Deep Dive 4 ends up having to solve.

scroll →

Why an on-disk append-only log? Sequential disk writes are nearly as fast as memory (~600MB/sec on modern SSDs). By only appending (never random writes), the message broker achieves 1M+ messages/sec per cluster across tens of partitions on commodity hardware - each individual partition has a single leader and is bounded by that sequential write ceiling. The OS page cache serves recent reads from memory transparently — no custom caching needed.

10. Data Modeling

On-Disk Log Segments (Broker Storage — message persistence):

Directory: /data/{topic}/{partition}/
  Segment files: 00000000000000000.log (1GB max per segment)
  Index files:   00000000000000000.index (sparse offset → file position mapping)
  Timeindex:     00000000000000000.timeindex (timestamp → offset mapping)

Each message on disk:
  [offset (8B)] [size (4B)] [crc (4B)] [magic (1B)] [key_len] [key] [value_len] [value] [headers]

Internal Compacted Topic (Offset Store — consumer positions):

Topic: __consumer_offsets (50 partitions)
  Key: (group_id, topic, partition)
  Value: { committed_offset, metadata, timestamp }
  Compaction: log-compacted (only latest per key retained)

Raft / KRaft (Metadata Store — cluster topology):

Stores: topic configs, partition assignments, broker registry, ACLs
Replicated via Raft consensus across controller quorum (3-5 nodes)
Access: strongly consistent reads for partition leader lookup

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Produce message Leader broker disk log Sequential append to segment file + replicate to ISR followers
Consume messages Leader broker + page cache Sequential read from offset — OS page cache serves recent data from RAM
Commit offset __consumer_offsets topic Produce to internal topic (compacted)
Find partition leader KRaft metadata Client fetches metadata → caches leader mapping locally
Replay from offset Broker disk Seek via index file → read sequentially from that position
scroll →

How a Message Is Durably Written with Replication:

  1. Producer sends message with acks=all to partition leader (Broker 1)
  2. Leader appends to local segment file (sequential write, ~10μs)
  3. Leader sends to in-sync replica (ISR) followers (Broker 2, 3). Each follower appends to their local log.💡 A replica is a second broker keeping its own copy of the same partition log. “In-sync” means it is currently caught up enough to be trusted to take over, which is what makes the handover on a crash safe. Learn more →
  4. Once all ISR followers ACK → leader increments High Watermark (HW)
  5. Leader responds to producer: “committed at offset 10542, partition 2”
  6. Only messages at or below HW are visible to consumers → guarantees no data loss on leader crash
  7. If leader crashes before follower ACKs: producer gets timeout, retries. Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) ensures exactly-once even on retry.

11. Deep Dives

1) A lost ack and a mid-batch crash both lose messages. How do we get to exactly-once?

Problem: FR1’s producer does not retry and FR2’s consumer commits before processing. Both ends drop messages on failure, in a system whose entire purpose is not dropping them.

Bad: at-most-once at both ends, which is what the high-level design shipped. The producer sends, gets an offset, and moves on; if that response is lost it never finds out whether the append happened, and does nothing. The consumer marks a batch done the moment it has it, so a crash mid-batch means nobody ever processes those messages.

Note the common property that makes this the worst kind of bug: both failures are silent. No error surfaces, no metric moves, no dead-letter queue fills. The producer believes it published, the consumer group believes it processed, and the messages are simply absent. You discover it from a downstream inconsistency weeks later with no log to reconstruct from.

The producer sends, gets an offset, and moves on; if that response is lost it never finds out whether the append happened, and does nothing. The consumer marks a batch done the moment it has it, so a crash mid-batch means nobody ever processes those messages.

Note the common property that makes this the worst kind of bug: No error surfaces, no metric moves, no dead-letter queue fills. The producer believes it published, the consumer group believes it processed, and the messages are simply absent. You discover it from a downstream inconsistency weeks later with no log to reconstruct from.

at-least-once. The producer retries until it gets an acknowledgement, and the consumer commits only processing. Nothing is lost now. What you get instead is duplicates, in two places: a retried publish that actually succeeded the first time appends the message twice, and a consumer that crashes between processing and committing reprocesses its batch on restart. For an idempotent consumer that is genuinely fine. For “charge this card” it is not.

The producer assigns a sequence number per partition. The broker deduplicates by (producer_id, sequence_number) — retried writes with the same sequence are . The consumer wraps processing + offset commit in a transaction — either both succeed or neither does. This gives true exactly-once end-to-end (Kafka 0.11+ supports this natively).

2) One broker owns the only copy of a partition. What happens when its disk dies?

Problem: FR1 appends to one log on one machine. Disks fail, machines fail, and a broker holding the only copy of a partition is a single point of data loss for everything in it.

Bad: no replication, exactly as FR1 built it. A broker loss takes every unread message in its partitions with it — and “unread” is the entire point, because a message queue’s whole job is holding things that have not been dealt with yet. The messages most likely to be lost are the ones nobody has processed, which is precisely the set that mattered.

It is also an availability failure, not just a durability one: the partition has no other owner, so producers writing to it fail and consumers reading from it stall until a human intervenes. At a few hundred brokers, disk failure is a weekly event rather than a hypothetical.

no replication, exactly as FR1 built it. A broker loss takes every unread message in its partitions with it — and “unread” is the entire point, because a message queue’s whole job is holding things that have not been dealt with yet. The messages most likely to be lost are the ones nobody has processed, which is precisely the set that mattered.

It is also an availability failure, not just a durability one: the partition has no other owner, so producers writing to it fail and consumers reading from it stall until a human intervenes. At a few hundred brokers, disk failure is a weekly event rather than a hypothetical.

Synchronous replication to N followers. Leader waits for ALL followers. Zero data loss but high latency and blocked by the slowest follower.

Leader tracks which followers are “in-sync” (caught up within a threshold). Writes are acknowledged when all ISR members have the data — not all replicas. Slow/failed followers are removed from ISR (writes continue). On leader failure, a new leader is elected from the ISR set (guaranteed to have all committed data). This balances durability (ISR size = replication factor) with availability (slow followers don’t block).

3) The log only ever grows. What deletes 86TB a day?

Problem: An append-only log is the right structure and it has no natural end. FR1 appends, FR3 adds partitions, and nothing anywhere removes a byte.

Bad: retain everything forever, which is what the high-level design does by omission. At 1M msg/sec and ~1KB per message that is 1GB/sec — about 86TB a day, so even a petabyte of provisioned disk is gone inside a fortnight.

The failure mode is worth being precise about, because it is not graceful. A full disk does not slow the broker down; it makes every append on every partition that broker owns fail at once. So the symptom is not “old messages unavailable”, it is a hard write outage across an arbitrary slice of the cluster, triggered by a clock rather than by load.

Time-based retention (delete segments older than 7 days). Simple but loses historical data.

4) payment_completed arrives before payment_created. Where did the ordering go?

Problem: FR2 guarantees ordering within a partition, and FR1 spreads each entity’s messages across all of them. Both are true, and together they guarantee nothing useful.

Bad: the round-robin partition assignment from FR1 step 1. It balances load beautifully and it is why the ordering guarantee is worthless: a single payment’s created, authorized and completed events land on three different partitions, consumed by three different consumers at three different rates. The consumer sees payment_completed before payment_created.

The subtle part is that the log was never wrong. Each partition is in perfect order, FR2’s exclusive assignment held, and every component did its job. The ordering was destroyed at routing time, before any of those guarantees applied — which is why this cannot be fixed anywhere downstream, and why a consumer that tries to reorder by timestamp is solving it in the wrong place.

The subtle part is that the log was never wrong. Each partition is in perfect order, FR2’s exclusive assignment held, and every component did its job. The ordering was destroyed at time, before any of those guarantees applied — which is why this cannot be fixed anywhere downstream, and why a consumer that tries to reorder by timestamp is solving it in the wrong place.

Key-based partitioning. All messages with the same key go to the same partition → strict ordering per key. Works perfectly until a (celebrity, viral product) overloads one partition.

Monitor per-partition throughput. When a partition is hot (one key dominates), either: (a) sub-partition that key across dedicated partitions with a secondary hash, or (b) accept slightly relaxed ordering for that specific key and process in parallel with sequence numbers for reordering at the consumer. LinkedIn uses approach (b) for high-volume activity streams.

5) One misbehaving producer can take down a broker for everyone. How do we bound it?

Problem: FR1’s broker accepts whatever arrives. There is no quota, no throttle and no rejection path, so the only thing limiting a producer is the producer’s own restraint.

Bad: accept everything, which is what FR1 does. A producer in a retry loop, a backfill job someone started on a Friday, or a bug that publishes inside a loop will all send faster than the broker can append. The broker buffers the excess in memory and then dies of it.

Two things make this worse than a single-tenant overload. A broker owns partitions from many topics, so one team’s runaway job kills unrelated teams’ pipelines — the blast radius has nothing to do with who caused it. And the failure is self-amplifying: the broker dies, its partitions get reassigned, the producers retry harder against the survivors, and the overload walks around the cluster.

accept everything, which is what FR1 does. A producer in a retry loop, a backfill job someone started on a Friday, or a bug that publishes inside a loop will all send faster than the broker can append. The broker buffers the excess in memory and then dies of it.

Two things make this worse than a single-tenant overload. A broker owns partitions from topics, so one team’s runaway job kills unrelated teams’ pipelines — the blast radius has nothing to do with who caused it. And the failure is self-amplifying: the broker dies, its partitions get reassigned, the producers retry harder against the survivors, and the overload walks around the cluster.

Broker rejects writes when a quota is exceeded (returns THROTTLED error). Producer retries with backoff.

Each producer/consumer is assigned a byte-rate quota by the broker (e.g., 50MB/sec produce, 100MB/sec consume). Broker tracks actual rate and delays responses proportionally when the quota is exceeded (adds artificial latency rather than hard-rejecting). This smooths traffic without the thundering-herd retries of hard rejection. Combined with consumer lag monitoring — if a consumer group falls too far behind, alert the team (the queue is growing unboundedly, which eventually hits retention limits and drops messages).

12. Design Self-Audit

  • Stale reads? Not applicable — consumers read from a single leader (strong ordering). Multi-region consumers may have follower-read lag but maintain ordering within their own stream.
  • Single points of failure? Leader failure triggers automatic election from ISR (seconds). ZooKeeper/KRaft is a dependency — mitigated by running 3-5 node quorum. No single-broker single point of failure (SPOF) for committed data.💡 A quorum is a majority of the group — 2 of 3, or 3 of 5. Requiring a majority to agree is what stops a network split from producing two controllers that each think they are in charge.
  • Dead-letter / reconciliation? Messages that repeatedly fail processing (poison pills) are redirected to a dead-letter topic after N retries. A separate consumer handles DLQ messages (alert + manual review).
  • Cost? Storage dominates at scale. With 1M msg/sec x 1KB avg x 7 days = ~600TB. On local SSD: ~$30K/month. With tiered storage (hot 1 day local, cold 6 days S3): ~$5K/month.
  • Hot partition? Monitored by broker metrics (bytes-in per partition). Mitigated by key distribution analysis at producer + partition rebalancing.

13. Core Flows

Flow 1: Produce with Replication

Non-obvious failure path: Follower 2 is slow (network issue). If it falls too far behind, the leader removes it from the ISR set. Now acks=all only requires Follower 1’s ACK. When Follower 2 catches up, it rejoins ISR. This prevents a slow follower from blocking all writes.

Flow 2: Consumer Rebalance (failure recovery)

Non-obvious failure: Consumer 2 crashed after processing messages but BEFORE committing offsets. Those messages will be redelivered to Consumer 1. The consumer must be idempotent (handle duplicates gracefully) or use exactly-once transactions.

14. Final Architecture

How it works end-to-end:

  1. Producers publish messages — clients send records to the appropriate broker (partition leader) via round-robin or key-based routing
  2. Broker appends to partition log — leader writes to its local append-only log and replicates to follower brokers
  3. Followers acknowledge — in-sync replicas confirm write; producer gets ack once replication factor is satisfied
  4. Controller manages metadata — KRaft quorum tracks partition leadership, broker liveness, and topic configuration
  5. Consumers pull messages — consumer group members are assigned partitions and read sequentially by offset
  6. Cold segments tiered to S3 — older log segments automatically moved to object storage to reduce broker disk costs while remaining queryable
